currentContext.business: The Company primarily sells prescription eyeglasses, sunglasses and other products such as contact lenses and eyewear accessories to retail (B2C) consumers seeking comprehensive vision care solutions. It commenced operations in India as an online business in 2010 and opened its first retail store in New Delhi in 2013, and today sells through retail stores, its websites, the Lenskart mobile application and other channels, with the websites and apps central to an omnichannel retailing presence powered by its technology platform. As of March 31, 2026 the Company operated 3,327 stores across 16 countries, with 2,609 stores in India, 287 in Japan, 284 in Southeast Asia, 41 in the Middle East and 106 stores in other geographies.

currentContext.expansion: Lenskart's expansion in FY26 was footprint-led rather than plant-led. The Company opened 603 net new stores globally, taking the network to 3,327 active stores across 16 countries as of March 31, 2026 - 2,609 stores in India, 287 in Japan, 284 in Southeast Asia, 41 in the Middle East and 106 in other geographies. International added only 61 net new stores, so most of the 30.2% international revenue growth was same-store-driven, and the Company has begun opening a few dedicated Meller brand stores to anchor the sunglasses category beyond shop-in-shop presence. Alongside stores, the India store mix continued to shift from FoFo to CoCo through FY26, reducing franchisee commission and incentive expense as a share of revenue. On the manufacturing side, operating cash flow funded the accelerated store rollout, store upgrades and manufacturing capex, including investment toward the Hyderabad facility; management states that growth and investment are both being funded from within the business. Supply-chain integration across Owndays and Meller is the other investment thread, with product margins in the most advanced markets such as Singapore and UAE trending toward approximately 80%, described as a repeatable pathway for further expansion. Omnichannel investments were made in Singapore, UAE and Thailand - app-led customer journeys, expanded online assortments and hyper-local innovations such as quick-commerce contact lens delivery - while Saudi Arabia and newer markets remain in an investment phase building the platform for future growth.
currentContext.mdna: India is a nascent, fast-growing category: over 700 million Indians require vision correction today against a market estimated at approximately `894 billion, with the addressable market growing at 13% and projected to exceed `4,000 billion by FY45|Management frames growth as demand creation rather than share shifting - every new eye test, every new Tier 2+ store and every first-time customer expands the market itself|Structural refractive-error burden: the affected population in India is estimated to exceed 943 million by 2030, with a significant proportion uncorrected due to affordability, awareness and access to optometry|Policy tailwind: the Government of India reduced GST on prescription eyeglasses and contact lenses from 12% to 5% in September 2025, making essential vision care more affordable|India macro was mixed in FY26 - GDP growth estimated at 6.3-6.8% but uneven consumption, urban demand slowed by retail inflation of 3.87% by March 2026 and high rental inflation, while organised experience-led retail was resilient with growth accelerating from 4-5% to 10-11% in the festive season|Vision correction is a recurring, essential and medical need that provides a natural hedge against a consumption slowdown, though the fashion element of the business may be more exposed|Currency and supply-side watch items: Rupee devaluation against key foreign currencies, supply chain disruptions and inflation pressure the import bill, logistics and raw material costs|International addressable pool: Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East together represent a `1,716 billion eyewear market in FY26, projected to reach `2,118 billion by FY30, with common traits of fragmentation, traditional-optician dominance, rising refractive error and limited D2C disruption|Organised and D2C segments are outpacing overall market growth - 10-14% in Southeast Asia, 7-10% CAGR in Japan and 15-20% in the Middle East (FY25-30) - as prescription eyewear priced 2-3x higher than India shifts consumers to affordable, high-quality players|Japan structural shift: D2C market share has climbed from 25% to 31% over five years and is projected to reach 43% by FY30, directly benefiting Owndays, which as the third-largest D2C player with 287 stores versus 500+ for the top two has substantial whitespace|Southeast Asia penetration gap mirrors India - about 65% of the population requires vision correction but only about 40% wear prescription glasses; in Singapore combined market share has grown from about 10% to 25% since the Owndays acquisition|Middle East demand is defined by high ASPs, a young digitally-native population and fashion-forward demand, with rapid movement toward omnichannel retail, though regional geopolitical tension brings supply chain uncertainty and imported-goods inflation|Eye tests are the leading indicator of the model - more eye tests lead to more first-time customers, more volume and more revenue, explaining the 24.7% growth in eyewear units sold and 22.6% growth in transacting customer accounts|Same-Pincode Sales Growth of 27.3% running 645 basis points above India SSSG of 20.8% is read by management as evidence that new stores create incremental demand rather than cannibalising existing ones|Customer franchise compounding: Gold members purchase at meaningfully higher frequency, with the FY23 cohort achieving 3.6 eyeglasses versus an India industry average of 1.8 over a two-year period, generating revenue without incremental acquisition cost|Premiumisation is lifting India ASP 6.3% YoY to `1,827 as customers choose better design, stronger lens features and more occasion-led products, while international ASP runs at roughly 3x India levels

risks.note: Increasing participation from organised and unorganised players across markets. Management's stated mitigation is the vertically integrated model with structural cost and speed advantages, plus brand pull that reduces dependence on promotional spending.

risks.risk: Macroeconomic fluctuations - currency, inflation and consumption slowdown
risks.note: Currency volatility, inflation and consumption slowdowns across markets. Management points to the essential, medical nature of prescription eyewear as natural demand resilience, 42% international revenue as currency diversification and backward integration to absorb input cost pressure; the MD&A separately flags Rupee devaluation raising the import bill, logistics and raw material costs, and notes the fashion element of the business is more exposed in a slowdown.

Dependence on specific manufacturing hubs and import corridors. Mitigation cited is multi-site manufacturing (Bhiwadi, Hyderabad, Thailand JV), progressive backward integration and RFID-enabled inventory visibility.

Risk of inconsistent customer experience as the store network scales rapidly. Mitigation is NPS-led feedback loops, AI-driven store operations, centralised training systems and self-service technology that reduces human variability.

Cybersecurity risks associated with customer data, facial recognition and AI systems; the BRSR separately identifies Data Privacy & Protection as a material risk where growing digital operations increase exposure, with breach costs, litigation, regulatory penalties and reputational damage as the stated financial implications.

risks.risk: Human capital - talent attraction, retention and high attrition
risks.note: Ability to attract, retain and develop specialised talent across geographies, mitigated through AI-enabled hiring, local-first international teams and an acqui-hire strategy. The BRSR discloses permanent-employee turnover of 51.4% in FY 2025-26 (53.9% in FY 2024-25 and 65.7% in FY 2023-24), a structurally high attrition rate for a workforce of 21,859 permanent employees globally.

risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance exposure across 16 countries
risks.note: Evolving regulations across 16 countries including data privacy, healthcare and trade policy. Mitigation is dedicated compliance teams per jurisdiction, proactive engagement with regulatory developments and diversified sourcing to mitigate trade policy risk.

Identified in the BRSR materiality table: climate-related regulations, carbon pricing and extreme weather events can affect operations and supply chains, with productivity losses and supply chain disruptions as the negative implication; the approach is renewable energy adoption, climate risk assessments and business continuity planning.

one-line thesis: Lenskart delivered record revenue and margin expansion driven by deep Tier 2+ market penetration and international scaling, with AI and smart eyewear now central to its next-phase growth; the compounding effect of vertical integration and store density is unlocking unprecedented profitability and customer acquisition efficiency.
financial scorecard: revenue: +41% YoY to ₹2,516cr; EBITDA/margin: +61% YoY to ₹322cr, margin +270bps to 21.3%; PAT (rptd): ₹204cr; PAT (normalized): ₹204cr (no distortions in Q4); order book: not disclosed; net debt: net cash of ₹3,881cr (post-IPO payables settled)
guidance: revenue growth: sustained double-digit (no specific %, but compounding expected); margin: long-term steady-state EBITDA pre-Ind AS target 25%; order inflow: no specific guidance; capex/commissioning: FY27 net new stores ~FY26 level (542), plus manufacturing investments
segment / subsidiary detail: India: revenue ₹1,475cr (+44% YoY), EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin 15.3% (+600bps), 170 net new stores, 6M eye tests, SSSG 24%, Same Pincode growth 31%; International: revenue ₹1,054cr (+35.4% YoY, +25% CC), EBITDA pre-Ind AS margin 9.2% (+110bps), 13 net new stores, Japan strongest performer, Middle East resilient
growth verticals / optionality: Tier 2+ towns (183 net new stores in Q4, 542 in FY26), international expansion (718 stores globally), smart glasses (B by Lenskart, 30K+ waitlist), AI-driven automation in eye testing and manufacturing, store densification in existing pin codes
margins & cost dynamics: India product margin held flat at 64% despite rupee depreciation due to vertical integration; cost savings from automation, HQ tech efficiency, and same-store growth drove EBITDA expansion; international margins improving via ACP reduction and scale
capex / expansion: ₹603cr funded by ₹887cr operating cash flow; included 603 net new stores, Hyderabad manufacturing facility, GeoIQ tech infrastructure
capital allocation: Prioritized store expansion, manufacturing (Hyderabad, Thailand JV), AI/R&D (smart glasses, automated eye testing), and M&A (Meller); net cash balance ₹3,881cr provides flexibility for future M&A or buybacks
risks & watch-items: currency volatility (rupee depreciation), geopolitical supply chain risks (mitigated by vertical integration), competitive entry in smart glasses (Google), execution risk in AI transformation, margin pressure from mass-market campaigns
management quality / tone: Highly confident, visionary, and execution-focused; emphasized long-term compounding, AI as core strategic shift, and patient capital allocation; dismissed short-term noise, stressed customer experience and volume growth over ASP
non-obvious takeaways: 1. 45% eye test growth vs 25% unit growth implies massive conversion upside; 2. Store clustering in same pin codes is not cannibalizing but expanding demand via micro-market optimization; 3. 64% product margin maintained despite rupee depreciation signals deep structural cost control; 4. Army cantonment store in Srinagar symbolizes untapped rural/semi-urban penetration

themes.title: Quick-commerce, omnichannel & retail expansion
themes.need: Quick-commerce and value retail are the structural growth engine, and Q1FY27 rewrote the unit-economics model. ETERNAL raised Blinkit's steady-state margin from a 5-6% range to ~6% and set a first-ever 4% GAAP EBIT margin target (after ESOP and depreciation) while capex per store went from INR 1cr to INR 2.5cr (+150%) with NOV/store/day up only 60% and net working capital improving 18 to 14 days - so margin can now drift DOWN while ROCE improves. Growth also decoupled from spend: Blinkit orders +21% QoQ with MTUs above 30mn achieved on LOWER marketing spend and fewer store adds, and management called Q1 the peak of competitive intensity to date. VMM did INR 3,727cr (+18.7%) on 10% SSSG with gross margin up to 28.7% driven by lower promotional spend rather than price hikes, validated a small-format store at the same revenue/sq ft and 'pretty much the same' ROCE as large format (a ~3,000-store national opportunity), and found 20% of its quick-commerce customers had never shopped a Vishal store. SHOPERSTOP swung PAT positive (+INR 5cr vs -INR 4cr) and raised FY27 LFL guidance from 5% to ~6%; ARVINDFASN lifted gross margin 90bps to 56.7% on full-price sell-through with direct channels now 62% of sales; MEESHO cut cost per delivered order ~INR 1 QoQ despite the May fuel hike. DMART/V2RETAIL/PATELRMART on value retail; TRENT-tier branded retail via ABFRL/METROBRAND/BATAINDIA/REDTAPE.
themes.driver: Blinkit dark-store rollout at the new INR 2.5cr/store capex against the 4% GAAP EBIT target; VMM small-format expansion; festive/quick-commerce GMV. Watch ARVINDFASN's SS27 sourcing lock (next 45-60 days) - if war-inflated input costs hold, apparel pricing corrects.
